### Introduction

This research is part of a series of reports which aim to collate and review current 
evidence on the potential environmental impacts and social implications of five 
greenhouse gas removal (GGR) technologies: ocean alkalinity enhancement, enhanced 
rock weathering (ERW), biochar, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), 
and direct air carbon capture and storage (DACCS). The carbon removal efficacy of the 
GGR technology, and the economic impacts of their implementation, is not explored in this 
project. 
This report synthesises the evidence related to the social implications of BECCS and 
highlights any evidence gaps. The findings in this report are based on a review of 
published and grey literature carried out in 2024. The approach to identifying, collating, 
and synthesising the available information on the social implications is described in the 
Appendix. 
A non-technical summary of this research is also provided as a separate document.

### Overview of BECCS

This section provides an overview of how the deployment of BECCS delivers carbon 
dioxide (CO2) removal from the atmosphere, detailing the various social constraints 
regarding implementation of the technology and brief context is provided on the current 
commercial maturity. 
The UK has committed to reducing carbon emissions by 80% by 2050. Biomass is 
anticipated to play a significant role in decarbonisation and GGR technologies including 
BECCS are expected to be deployed at an increasing rate and scale. 
The scale of implementation is expected to be limited by the availability of land and the 
robustness of biomass supply chains capable of supporting an increased rate of bioenergy 
production (RS & RAE, 2018). BECCS has a policy advantage in its cost-effective 
production of low-carbon energy and versatility to be implemented in a variety of locations 
(Fajardy & MacDowell, 2018). Both characteristics lead to BECCS having the largest 
modelled contribution to CO2 removals through 2050 (RS & RAE, 2018; BEIS, 2021b). 
However, cost-efficiency is lowered if BECCS is established in locations further from 
energy crop and geologic storage sources (Asibor et al., 2021), and the economic 
advantages may conflict with the GGR potential if reduced energy costs are prioritised (RS 
& RAE, 2018). 
The successful deployment and integration of BECCS requires consideration of specific 
local infrastructures, biomass sources, socio-economic characteristics, existing energy 
systems, land management strategies and political and geographic contexts (Freer et al., 
2022; Clery et al., 2021). 

#### Description

Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage is a combination of two distinct technologies to deliver GGRs: bioenergy and carbon capture and storage (CCS). Bioenergy utilises the natural photosynthesis process by which plants and trees absorb CO2 as they grow to produce biomass which is combusted to generate energy. CCS is then utilised to capture released carbon from the conversion process and secure it in long-term storage. BECCS projects to date largely involve retrofitting existing power plants that use biomass as a feedstock, using post-combustion carbon capture technology. Other capture technologies expected to be used include pre-combustion gasification and oxyfuel combustion. The technological readiness level (TRL) of BECCS varies depending on its use: a TRL of 5 for hydrogen production and 7 for heat and energy production, where 9 indicates the highest level of readiness (BEIS, 2021b). There is currently only one commercial, full-scale BECCS plant in operation in the US with another in formal discussions for development in the UK (Brack & King, 2021; Drax, 2023b). As well as delivering a net removal of CO2, the BECCS process offers a source of electricity through bioenergy rather than fossil fuels. This distinguishes BECCS from many

7 of 43

other GGR technologies, as it can support both energy and climate targets. The UK 
government has set a target for BECCS to remove 52-58 Mt CO2/year and provide 
between 75-350 TWh of electricity output for CCS operations by 2050 (DESNZ, 2023). In 
2021, bioenergy generated 12.6% of UK electricity, up from 4.6% in 2012 (BEIS, 2021a; 
Booth & Wentworth, 2023), with expectations for this to continue growing as the UK moves 
towards net zero carbon emissions. 
The scaling up of BECCS will require consideration of impacts to energy markets and 
unintended social consequences (RS & RAE, 2018). Consumption of limited 
environmental resources such as water and land may lead to socio-economic implications, 
but government policy could play an important role in distributing the burden and benefits 
associated with each stage of the BECCS life cycle equitably. It is important that potential 
hazards are clearly understood at the outset. A strategic plan for the UK that maximises 
CO2 removal while minimising wider social implications through control measures and 
monitoring across BECCS’ operational lifetime should be commissioned and 
communicated through a public consultation.

### Social Implications

This section explores the actual and potential social implications of BECCS identified within existing evidence, and identifies where there are research gaps. The analysis is structured around the four key life-cycle stages of BECCS:

• Feedstock sourcing – obtaining biomass materials such as agricultural residues, forestry residues, dedicated energy crops, and waste biomass. 
• Feedstock processing and transport – converting the biomass materials into a form ready for power plants e.g. pelletisation. 
• Feedstock Conversion – burning the biomass materials at power plants. 
• Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) – capturing the carbon emitted during the conversion stage and securely storing it. 
• Social acceptability – public opinions of BECCS and the factors that can influence these both positively and negatively. 
• Socio-economic implications – potential economic benefits, employment opportunities, and wider human health implications of BECCS operations. 
• Government policy – brief exploration into the wider social implications of policy and governance over the deployment of BECCS. 

The following social implications identified within the available evidence are examined under each life-cycle stage:

##### Feedstock sourcing Social acceptability

Imported biomass 
The social acceptability of biomass for BECCS depends on the sourcing location of the 
feedstock, with imported biomass being more contentious than domestic biomass. For the 
UK, this is important to consider as 34% of biomass feedstock used in renewable energy 
production is imported: 60% from the United States, 16% from Canada, and 18% from the 
EU (DESNZ, 2023; NAO, 2024). Woody biomass comprised 61% of all biomass imports in 
2022, including 7.5 million tonnes of wood pellets imported for renewable energy 
production (DESNZ, 2023). 
In a social study conducted in Oxfordshire the support for imported biomass was mixed, 
with 51.5% in opposition and 48.5% in support (Bellamy et al., 2019). Opposing 
participants stated that “deforestation outweighs the benefits gained from increase in 
biomass” and it “adds emissions to the equation” that may make the process 
counterproductive. The opposing participants raised additional concerns and potential 
challenges around the scalability of the technology, land-use changes, geographical 
footprint, and public costs associated with BECCS. 
One challenge posed by those who oppose imported biomass focused on the 
sustainability and longevity of international biomass sources. At a scaled-up rate, BECCS 
may rely on long term supply contracts for energy dense biomass from other nations, who 
are also likely to begin implementing BECCS (DESNZ, 2023) which could pose a risk to 
the UK’s long-term BECCS strategy. Those who support imported biomass state that 
additional feedstock stability can be found domestically with 66% of the biomass used in 
UK heat, electricity and transport originating from domestic sources (NAO, 2024). These 
domestic sources are comprised of 35% mixed biomass (straw, wood pellets and
